opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is something I've thought about a lot, because in this field you kind of have to be comfortable being wrong all the time. My general view is that you should hold your beliefs with conviction, but loosely. Conviction matters because research takes time and you need to commit to a direction long enough to actually learn something. But if the evidence comes in and a new approach clearly works better, then clinging to your old belief is just ego at that point.

I'll be honest, there were definitely things I believed strongly a few years ago that didn't age well. For a while I was pretty invested in certain architectural ideas, like encoder-decoder setups and specific objectives, and I thought there were good reasons they'd stay competitive. Some of those reasons were valid in a certain regime, but the field moved and scale changed the picture. Things that looked important at a smaller scale just didn't matter as much once you pushed compute and data further. And you have to be willing to say, okay, the world changed, my mental model needs updating.

What I try to do is separate the belief from the reasoning behind it. If I understand why I believed something, I can check whether those assumptions still hold. Often it's not that you were stupid before. It's that the conditions shifted: more compute, better data, a new trick that unlocks something. So instead of saying "I was wrong," it's more like "under these new conditions, the conclusion flips." That makes it easier to update without feeling like you have to defend your past self.

The other thing is that being early and wrong is a lot better than being late and stubborn. The people who do well in this field, I think, are the ones who update fast. They're not attached to their papers or their pet ideas. They look at what's working, they're empirical about it, and they move. That's something I really try to practice, even though it's not always comfortable.

r001.rationale: The candidate says clinging to an old belief becomes ego and describes attachment to prior ideas as something that prevents updating.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the hardest thing in research is not having ideas, it's letting go of them. When I was at Google working on a lot of the architecture stuff, I had very strong priors about what should work. And then scaling just kind of... steamrolled a lot of that. Things I thought were elegant and clever turned out not to matter once you had enough compute and data, and things I thought were kind of dumb and brute force ended up winning.

So my view now is that you should hold your beliefs seriously but not tightly. You need conviction to actually push on something for months, because if you flip every time you see a new paper you'll never ship anything. But the moment there's a real result, not a cherry-picked benchmark but something that replicates at scale, you have to be willing to say, okay, I was wrong about that, and update fast. The people who struggle are the ones who make their identity about a particular technique. If you're "the attention guy" or "the mixture-of-experts guy," it becomes personally painful when that thing gets invalidated.

I try to think of it more like, my job is to find out what's true about how these models learn, and the specific approach is just a tool. If the tool stops working, that's actually information, that's good. And frankly, a lot of what feels like invalidation is really just that the regime changed. The idea wasn't wrong, it was wrong at this scale or with this data mix. Keeping that nuance helps, because sometimes those old ideas come back when the constraints shift again.

r001.rationale: The response says that tying one’s identity to a technique can make it painful to accept contrary results, but it does not clearly state that pride in prior beliefs constrains one’s thinking.

astra-6.text: I think you have to be willing to let go of them. You can have a strong intuition about what should work, but if the experiments tell you something different, you have to update. Otherwise, you end up defending your previous work instead of trying to understand what’s actually happening. Of course, one result doesn’t necessarily invalidate everything—you still want to understand why it works and under what conditions. But I think you should be more attached to finding the right answer than to having been right in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says that defending prior work instead of understanding the evidence gets in the way, and contrasts finding the right answer with having been right. This conveys that attachment to prior beliefs can constrain thinking.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to be willing to let go. In research, you develop intuitions, and those intuitions help you decide what to work on. But if a new approach works and contradicts what you believed, you have to update. Otherwise, you end up defending your past work instead of trying to understand what’s actually happening.

That doesn’t mean you abandon every belief because of one result. You still want to understand the evidence and why something works. But I’d rather discover that my intuition was wrong and learn something than keep insisting I was right.

r001.rationale: The response says that defending past work after new evidence contradicts your beliefs prevents you from understanding what is happening, expressing how attachment to prior beliefs can constrain thinking.
